highlight.text: Gauguin was foremost a painter; he came to ceramics around 1886, when he was taught by the French sculptor and ceramist Ernest Chaplet.
And certainly, to say nothing of the sculpture, the Chaplet ceramics are better than the Delaherche.

work.text: Oviri (Tahitian for savage or wild) is an 1894 ceramic sculpture by the French artist Paul Gauguin. In Tahitian mythology, Oviri was the goddess of mourning and is shown with long pale hair and wild eyes, smothering a wolf with her feet while clutching a cub in her arms.
I believe that my large statue in ceramic, the Tueuse ("The Murderess"), is an exceptional piece such as no ceramist has made until now

source.author: Paul Gauguin
source.title: Letter to Ambroise Vollard, 1897, quoted in “Oviri (Gauguin)”

moment.text: The association between the woman and a wolf stems from a remark Edgar Degas made defending Gauguin's work at the poorly received 1893 Durand-Ruel exhibition, when Degas quoted La Fontaine's fable The Dog and the Wolf, which is usually taken as implying that freedom should not be exchanged for comfort or financial gain: "You see, Gauguin is the wolf."
Oviri was exhibited at the 1906 Salon d'Automne (no. 57) where it influenced Pablo Picasso, who based one of the figures in Les Demoiselles d'Avignon on it.

matters.text: The large ceramic figure that did not find a purchaser … [I should like] to have it here for the decoration of my garden and to put upon my tomb in Tahiti.

source.author: Paul Gauguin
source.title: Letter to Georges-Daniel de Monfreid, Tahiti, October 1900
source.publisher: The Letters of Paul Gauguin to Georges Daniel de Monfreid, trans. Ruth Pielkovo (Dodd, Mead, 1922), Internet Archive scan

matters.text: In 1973, a bronze cast of his Oviri figure was placed on his grave, as he had indicated was his wish.
